content: Exercise-induced anaphylaxis (EIA) is a condition in which anaphylactic symptoms are triggered by physical activity. In these individuals, neither the ingestion of the triggering agent alone nor exercise alone is sufficient to cause anaphylaxis. Common triggering agents include foods such as celery, wheat, soy protein, cheese, and shellfish, as well as medications like aspirin and other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). Wheat-dependent exercise-induced anaphylaxis (WDEIA) is a specific form of EIA caused by an IgE-mediated allergic reaction to the ω-gliadin component of wheat gluten. This reaction can also involve homologous proteins found in certain subspecies of wheat, such as those with the Aegilopides speltoides genome BB. WDEIA is distinct from gluten intolerance and is more closely related to another condition called baker's asthma. Both WDEIA and baker's asthma involve the IgE subclass of immunoglobulins, but their triggers differ. Baker's asthma is caused by the inhalation of wheat flour, while WDEIA is triggered by the presence of wheat gliadin peptides in the bloodstream during exercise or after prolonged use of aspirin or NSAIDs, such as ibuprofen. Unlike gluten sensitivity, WDEIA does not appear to involve rye or barley glutens. The IgE antibodies in patients with WDEIA specifically recognize the omega-gliadin (Gli-B1) protein encoded by the gene located on chromosome 1B of wheat. Additionally, the allergic responses observed in patients with wheat-dependent urticaria seem to closely resemble those seen in WDEIA.
